editorial_status: Political satire revision for user review; humor is not automatically certified

political_review_flags.lead: At a travelling workers’ fair, Florida roofers show your crew the law blocking local heat protections. Their protest canopy covers the water cooler. A sponsor praising deregulation has put his chair underneath it. The roofers need help moving the display.

A community volunteer flags down your van with letters about the Pentagon accepting Qatar’s luxury jet. Her workplace made her declare a gifted muffin. She offers some food for a recorded reply. Her copy of the form asks whether the muffin has foreign owners.

Workers protesting their employer’s no-tip rule have built a cardboard jet after the Pentagon accepted Qatar’s plane. They flag your crew down for testimony or a hand pushing it. The wings are made from rejected gift declarations. One used to be about a biscuit.

Hotel workers invite your stopped crew to an upstairs meeting about their employer’s ban on guest gifts. They’re comparing a confiscated biscuit with the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The lift is reserved for management. The biscuit has been allowed to use it as evidence.

At a roadside hall, residents invite your crew to a standing-room meeting about officials sharing Yemen strike details in Signal. Public questions must be handwritten, checked, and submitted upstairs. A volunteer has already lost the pencil. It has better access than the audience.

A travelling trade fair celebrates Florida’s ban on local heat mandates with a “voluntary break” treadmill. Your hot crew stops beside it. The water cooler moves farther away whenever the belt turns. A roofer offers shade and asks for water donations.

After the Pentagon accepted Qatar’s luxury jet, a roadside workers’ fair built a gift-inspection tunnel. Your crew is invited to compare it with their employer’s strict gift rule. A muffin cannot pass. The aircraft-shaped hole behind it is generously proportioned.

Your crew stops at a temp-work desk. The recruiter’s no-gifts briefing runs beneath a report about the Pentagon accepting Qatar’s jet. She seals a complimentary mint in an evidence bag. “Vendor influence.” The mint has achieved a level of scrutiny unavailable to most aircraft.

Your aching crew stops at a temp-work briefing. The recruiter’s gift policy requires workers to document a free coffee while a news display covers the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The coffee has its own folder. Applicants are still standing. A volunteer welcomes supply donations.

A temp-work centre sells some food for $6 and offers your crew $10 to inventory gifts surrendered under its employer’s rule. Above the mint collection, a news screen reports the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The recruiter has ordered a bigger evidence bag. For the mints.

Florida barred local heat-break rules. At a roadside trade fair, a contractor wants the same freedom here. He praises toughness from inside a refrigerated sales trailer. A worker points you toward shade; the trailer’s exhaust is blowing directly onto her.

Florida blocked local heat-break mandates. At a gym open house, a contractor promotes copying the law while workers assemble his enormous cooling fan. Nine dollars pays for moving its bases. Showers are free with your own soap; apparently water works better without a speech.

Florida barred local heat-break mandates. At a mountain-region contractors’ fair, a speaker urges copying the law. A technician offers $10 to sort parts beside the speaker’s personal cooling unit. The technician would like workers classified as equipment worth preventing from overheating.

Florida banned local heat-break mandates. At a desert trade stall promoting that approach, the water cooler has been placed inside a locked display cage. An installer offers water for clearing access or $12 for moving heavy barriers. The speaker calls this freedom from interference.

Florida barred local heat-break mandates; a desert contractor wants that model here. At his hiring table, he offers $12 to carry refill crates while mist cools his chair. He calls compulsory water breaks government overreach. His misting nozzle has three settings.

Florida barred local heat-break mandates; a desert yard supervisor promotes copying it. He offers $10 to shift the heavy temperature display into shade before his press photo. A worker has the earlier readings and room beneath a shade cloth. The workers remain in the sun.
Near a Billings public building, a seamstress waits beside the travelers with some mending.
Outside Boise City Hall, a delivery rider tells the travelers about the 2025 flag dispute.
Near Wyoming’s Capitol, a roofer shares a lunch bench with the travelers.
At a Cumberland supermarket, a home-care aide discusses Maryland’s leave timetable with the travelers.
At a Dallas laundromat, a renter compares housing costs while the van blankets dry.
On a Flagstaff evening walk, a night cleaner stops where the stars show above the shops.
At a Frederick laundromat, a cleaner compares rental applications while your clothes tumble.
At a Joplin diner booth, a cleaner sorts pay slips beside a property-sale advertisement.
At a Las Vegas shaded water stop, a groundskeeper sets down a dusty rake.
At a Phoenix bus stop, a delivery worker shifts with the narrow shadow of a pole.
At a Pittsburgh diner exit, an off-duty server pockets a work schedule.
At a Pittsburgh overlook, a window cleaner rests beside your food bag.
At a Rapid City roadside overlook, a carpenter talks about the Black Hills treaty.
Near Salt Lake City Hall, a seamstress pauses while you rest on the steps.
At a San Antonio park bench, a construction worker explains what stood before HemisFair.
At Toledo’s Glass City Metropark, a groundskeeper rests while you share some food.
At a Tucson park drinking fountain, a groundskeeper explains the separate irrigation system.
At a Tulsa bus-stop bench, a school bus driver compares the state’s video order with your route.
By Waco’s suspension bridge, a delivery driver pauses while you eat some food.
During an unloading shift, {name} becomes dehydrated. The boss praises Florida’s ban on local heat-break rules. “Government shouldn’t tell us what to do,” he says, blocking the water.
Your contact {name} sends a video claiming journalists invented the Signal scandal, then blocks the crew. The explanation is now more secure than the bombing chat.
At a foraging walk, the guide says lobbyists get dinner for discussing food policy. You’ll be getting dinner from a bush. The bush has fewer sponsors.
Heavy rain hits as the radio celebrates climate-policy rollbacks. The announcement is waterproof. The passenger-side window isn’t.
The radio plays “Drill, baby, drill” over another heat warning. The dashboard has begun producing its own plastic reserves.
A heat wave arrives. On the radio, an official opposes worker heat rules from a room you can hear being air-conditioned.
Cold grips the route. The fossil-fuel lobby calls its dinner an energy-security event. You’d like to attend the room-temperature portion.
Smoke hangs over the road. The radio celebrates rolling back environmental rules. You close the windows on the celebration.

You know how Washington sells access. Unfortunately, your five companions know how much gas costs. You leave Los Angeles for D.C. with lobbying experience and a donor network consisting of the glove box.
You win the hearing. The chair calls it a triumph of American greatness. He is already editing out the part where you had to argue with him.
The final vote goes against you. You brought evidence, testimony and an actual journey. The donor envelope brought none of these and gets invited to dinner.
The van is destroyed and the expedition ends. Calling it a tank did no more than calling defense “war.” At least the scrap yard uses names that describe the contents.
Weather ends the expedition. The fossil-fuel speech promises an economy without environmental obstacles. Outside the van, an obstacle has become the entire view.
The breakdown ends the journey. Washington can rename defense “war” and call the job done. Your van’s newly impressive title still needs a functioning part beneath it.
Disease ends the journey. Washington can describe projected health-spending cuts as savings. The budget looks much healthier when none of the sick people are drawn on the chart.
Panic ends the journey. The government has renamed defense “war” to make everyone feel safer. The word “relax” could probably use a less heavily armed communications team.
This journey is unfinished. In Washington, the donor dinner is still on the calendar. The chicken has secured an appointment; your case is still on the road.
